title: Curiosity Loop: life, death, transformation, return
concept: The spiral as a continuous movement through states of being. It opens at the centre with birth and emergence, widens through growth, erodes through death and loss, and turns into rebirth, memory and ancestry, ending on the same Kongo cosmogram it began with, so the viewer realises the exhibition has been moving in a circle. References: Hilma af Klint, the Kongo cosmogram (dikenga dia Kongo), Robert Smithson and Ana Mendieta. Smithson and Mendieta are still in copyright, so the Death section uses public-domain works that echo their ideas (entropy, shifting earth, ruin, the body returning to the land) rather than their images.

works.description: Made centuries after Catholicism became the Kongo Kingdom's official faith, this crucifix gives Christ braids like a Kongo man. The x-shape incised into his waist wrapper references the dikenga dia Kongo, a symbol that diagrams the life cycle's four points.

works.description: From the first group of Hilma af Klint's Paintings for the Temple, begun in 1906. Green and gold coils spiral inward on a deep blue ground, picturing the world at its origin.
Philipp Otto Runge's four-part print series Times of Day represents not only the four times of day but also the seasons and the stages of human life.
The first plate of Jan Muller's engraved series The Creation of the World, showing the first day, when darkness was separated from light.
One of four prints of the biblical parable of the sower. Here the sower finds fertile soil for his seed, resulting in the bountiful harvest seen in the background.
Ancient Egyptian men and women loved cosmetics, and the objects that held them were given lavish treatment. Here the fanciful form is an ostrich egg.
The earth goddess Ge (also known as Gaia) hands her baby, Erichthonios, to Athena. Erichthonios would go on to become a king of Athens.

Attributed to the Yombe peoples, this mother and child figure's naturalism suggests that it could have been the portrait of a real person.
Johanna Helena Herolt, the daughter of Maria Sibylla Merian, painted a poppy in three stages of flowering together with a caterpillar, pupa and butterfly.
Day, from Philipp Otto Runge's Times of Day, a four-part series that also represents the seasons and the stages of human life.
Nautilus shells were brought to the Netherlands from Indonesia. Skilled Dutch silversmiths mounted them in silver, creating luxurious vessels sought after by wealthy collectors.

works.description: Adulthood, the seventh panel of Hilma af Klint's The Ten Largest. Large yellow forms swell at the center, surrounded by smaller shapes and script-like lines.
After three trips to Central and South America, Martin Johnson Heade made a large number of paintings of birds and flowers, especially orchids, in a tropical setting.
The twists and turns, ebb and flow of the natural form of the tree root can be interpreted as the energy that gives life and the endless transformations in the universe.

works.description: The last of Hilma af Klint's The Ten Largest. In Old Age, four colored fields sit inside a calm grid on a pale pink ground.
Evening, from Philipp Otto Runge's Times of Day, a four-part series that also represents the seasons and the stages of human life.
The massive silvery trunk of a dead tree juts from a dune. In Jacob van Ruisdael's landscapes, dead trees, waterfalls, and ruined buildings were visual expressions of the passage of time.
A desolate place discovered by a lonely explorer: the framing blocks the horizon and shows a single wagon, the photographer's converted portable darkroom, and only two sets of footprints.

Teynard sets the colossal sculptures of Abu Simbel into the context of large cliffs and vast expanses of desert. The temple was relocated in 1968 to prevent its submersion; this view no longer exists.
An imagined scene of a ruined ancient city bathed in the nostalgic glow of twilight.

Made for a burial in Roman Egypt, where mummification created a physical "duplicate" for the soul to rest in. Golden lips and jewelry may have been meant to transform the spirit, not to beautify the mortal body.
This power figure once hosted a spirit after priests placed empowering substances inside it. When the nkisi had served its purpose, the materials were removed, stripping it of its spiritual power.
This lidded jar once contained the cremated remains of the dead. Burial jars of this type became widespread after the introduction of Buddhism, as cremation became a common practice in Korea.
One of Vishnu's two wives, Bhu, the earth goddess, holds the lotus in her left hand.
Night, from Philipp Otto Runge's Times of Day, a four-part series that also represents the seasons and the stages of human life.
A carved jade cicada. Cicadas emerge from the earth after years underground, and in ancient Chinese art they came to be associated with rebirth.
Amulets like the heart scarab were placed in a mummy's wrappings to protect the deceased during their journey in the afterlife. The scarab beetle was an Egyptian symbol of renewal.

Maria Sibylla Merian reared caterpillars herself to study their life cycles. This drawing portrays the life cycle of the European pink-spotted hawk moth as well as its favorite food, the morning glory.

works.description: From Hilma af Klint's series The Swan, which explores opposites meeting and merging. A many-colored form joins a white sphere above and a brown sphere below.
Her miter-shaped hairstyle, chiseled teeth, and raised body scars signal that the woman incarnates the founding ancestor of a kinship group.
Thirty figures from various generations of ancestors, men on the right and women on the left. Scrolls of this type were displayed for worship at home during the New Year celebrations.

Around the central knob are four leaves, a ring of tiny beads, and a circle of small lotus flower designs; outside them, eight petal shapes each hold a Sanskrit letter.
